blocks.text: Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This

American photographer Susan kae Grant has made dreams her material and her photographic territory. Night Journey , published by MW Editions, is the culmination of a life’s work: a sumptuous and haunting volume, in black and white, crafted with the precision of a haute couturière of the unconscious.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Susan kae Grant.

Susan kae Grant grew up in a small town in Wisconsin. A shy and silent child, she expressed herself by drawing, writing, and making collages. Alfred Hitchcock and Rod Serling, creator of the anthology series The Twilight Zone , served as her compass: “the way they created mystery came through tormented theatrical storytelling.”

Trained in photography at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, she went on to teach photography at Texas Woman’s University for thirty-six years. Her artistic lineage connects her to what critic A.D. Coleman called the “directorial mode” — a photography in which the scene is entirely constructed by the photographer, in the tradition of Duane Michals, master of narrative sequence, and Arthur Tress, explorer of childhood dreams and nightmares.

In the 1990s, Susan kae Grant agreed to have electrodes placed on her body and to be awakened during REM sleep to describe aloud what she had just seen. Listening back to the recordings, she discovered a voice she barely recognized, phrases spoken in an in-between state, neither fully asleep nor truly awake. “I realized that these recordings had been made in a different state of consciousness.” The words murmured in the dark — “She’s Afraid to Stop”, “Something Needs Constant Attention”, “We Act Like We Don’t Know One Another” — would become the titles of her photographs.

In her Dallas studio, Susan kae Grant works with a 4×5 camera fitted with a digital back. Rare in contemporary photography, she never photographs her subjects directly — only the shadows they cast. She layers models, props, and floral wire, repositioning directional lights dozens of times, sometimes over months, for a single image.

This shadow theater summons Murnau’s Nosferatu and German Expressionism as much as Plato’s allegory of the cave. “It’s like being inside a gigantic three-dimensional photogram that I can’t fully see until I’m behind the camera,” she explains. “I strive to design sets with a sense of mystery and ambiguity, to provoke a narrative that raises more questions than it answers.”

The silhouettes that populate her images have no faces. These anonymous bodies fall, embrace, reach toward something just out of frame. As essayist Deborah Willis writes in the book’s opening essay titled Mapping the Dream Terrain , these figures “function less as characters than as vessels for sensation and memory,” inviting the viewer to project their own nights onto the page. “The narratives are a representation of a representation, and they exist only in the imagination.”

Founder of The Black Rose Press since 1976, Susan kae Grant has produced twelve limited-edition artist books, held in the collections of the Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Night Journey is their crowning achievement. With its gatefolds, triptychs, and an entire section printed on translucent paper where images layer like strata of memory, the book performs, down to its very design, the logic of the dream.
Night Journey by Susan kae Grant is published by MW Editions and available for $70.
